title: Minimum Wage Effects Across State Borders: Estimates Using Contiguous Counties
research_question: What are the effects of minimum wage increases on earnings and employment in low-wage sectors, particularly the restaurant industry, in the United States? Do minimum wage hikes produce adverse employment effects, and how do estimated effects depend on whether comparisons account for local economic conditions and spatial heterogeneity in employment trends?
data_description: The primary data source is the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW), based on ES-202 unemployment insurance filings covering approximately 98% of U.S. workers. The authors construct a panel of quarterly county-level employment and average weekly earnings for full-service restaurants (NAICS 7221) and limited-service restaurants (NAICS 7222), as well as accommodation and food services, retail, and manufacturing. The sample spans 1990q1 through 2006q2 (66 quarters) across 48 mainland U.S. states. Two analytic samples are used: an all-counties sample of 1,380 counties with balanced panels (91,080 observations) and a contiguous border county-pair sample of 504 border counties forming 316 pairs. State and federal minimum wage data come from the U.S. Department of Labor. County population data come from the Census Bureau. County Business Patterns data and the Current Population Survey are used for robustness checks.
institutional_context: Between 1990 and 2006, U.S. minimum wage policy varied substantially across states and over time. The federal minimum wage changed in 1991-1992 and 1996-1997, while the number of states setting minimum wages above the federal floor grew from 3 in 1990 to 32 in 2006. This created persistent wage gaps of 7-20% between adjoining states sharing a border, with 288 contiguous county-pairs experiencing minimum wage differentials at some point. Restaurants are the most intensive users of minimum wage labor: in 2006 they employed roughly 30% of all workers paid within 10% of the minimum, and about a third of restaurant workers earned near-minimum wages. Low-wage employment growth varied considerably across U.S. regions during this period, with the South growing faster despite having no state minimum wages, motivating concerns that nationwide comparisons conflate minimum wage effects with unrelated regional economic trends.
